system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2174-07-14 21:17:00 to 2174-07-16 15:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  History of primary sclerosing cholangitis with fever and reports
of abnormal LFTs in an outside hospital.

COMPARISON:  MR abdomen ___.

FINDINGS:  The liver texture is echogenic consistent with fatty infiltration. 
A more hypoechoic area at the superior right lobe may represent an area of
focal fatty sparing.  The two mobile stones are seen within the gallbladder
which is not dilated with no gallbladder wall thickening or pericholecystic
fluid.  There is no intra- or extra-hepatic biliary dilatation.  The bile duct
measures 5 mm in diameter.  Visualized portions of the head of the pancreas
are normal.  The body and tail are obscured by overlying bowel gas.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Echogenic liver consistent with fatty infiltration, more advanced forms of
liver disease cannot be ruled out on the basis of this study.
2.  Gallstones without evidence of cholecystitis.
3.  No intra- or extra-hepatic biliary dilatation.

INDICATION:  PSC, assess for fevers.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1- and T2-weighted images were acquired on a 1.5 T
magnet including dynamic 3D imaging obtained prior to, during, and after the
uneventful intravenous administration of 0.1 mmol/kg gadolinium-DTPA.

FINDINGS:  Extensive intrahepatic bile duct irregularity is present, this has
somewhat progressed since previous imaging, in particular in the left
intrahepatic ducts.  Beading and stricturing is noted and there is extensive
peribiliary enhancement.  A linear area of soft tissue enhancemenet is also
present anterior to the portal vein confluence (series 12, image 27 through to
25), likely a track of inflammatory tissue.  These features are suggestive of
significant active ongoing inflammation. No focal mass is present.  The common
bile duct maximally measures 6 mm.  No gallstones are present.

The kidneys, adrenal glands and spleen are normal.  Ductus divisum is noted. 
Pancreas is otherwise normal.

IMPRESSION: Significant intrahepatic bile duct irregularity consistent with
known diagnosis of PSC which has progressed since previous imaging since ___.
Avid peribiliary enhancement is noted in addition to enhancing tissue adjacent
to the portal vein confluence.  These features are suggestive of active
ongoing inflammation. No definitive evidence of tumor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospital doctors. You're here because of abdominal pain and fever. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I woke up yesterday with sharp pain under my right rib. It hasn’t gone away. I also had a fever at home, around 100.6, and I’ve been nauseous—eating makes it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any vomiting, diarrhea, or yellowing of your skin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I haven’t thrown up or had any changes in my bowel movements. No yellowing either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of primary sclerosing cholangitis, or PSC, we’re concerned this could be a flare-up or an infection in the bile ducts—what we call cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that sounds serious. Could it be related to my gallstones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked with an ultrasound. You do have gallstones, but no signs of gallbladder inflammation. The good news is your bile duct isn’t dilated, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain and fever then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not completely sure yet. Your liver enzymes are elevated, which suggests some liver or bile duct irritation. We’re going to start you on IV antibiotics just in case it’s cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been on ursodiol for years—should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue your ursodiol, along with your other regular meds like levothyroxine and lisinopril. We’ll review everything daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my celiac disease—I’m still on a gluten-free diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll make sure your meals are gluten-free. We also saw your liver looks echogenic on ultrasound—consistent with fatty infiltration—but we need more detail.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean my liver is getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It can be seen in PSC. But to be safe, we’ve scheduled an MRCP tomorrow to get a better look at your bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve had those before. Will it show if my PSC is progressing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’ll help us see if there’s new narrowing or inflammation. For now, rest and let the antibiotics work. We’ll check your labs in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white blood cell count is normal, and your liver enzymes are already trending down—ALT and AST are lower than yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? My pain is a bit better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. No sign of infection in your blood, but we did find gram-positive bacteria in your urine. It’s likely not the main issue, but we’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should we treat that too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wait for culture results. For now, the focus is your liver and bile ducts. Your MRCP is scheduled for later today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve reviewed your MRCP results. There’s no blockage or tumor, but there is active inflammation in your bile ducts—more than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my PSC is getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s progression in the left ducts, with beading and strictures. But no cancer. The inflammation explains your symptoms. We’ll continue antibiotics to cover possible cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the antibiotics help with the inflammation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They won’t reverse the structural changes, but they’ll treat any infection contributing to the flare. We’ll switch you to oral ciprofloxacin tomorrow so you can go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I can go home soon. How long do I take the cipro?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Twelve days total. We’ll give you a prescription. Also, keep taking your ursodiol—it helps slow PSC progression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—omeprazole, levothyroxine, the supplements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your regular medications. No changes except adding the cipro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I follow up with my gastroenterologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in two weeks. They’ll review the MRCP and decide if any adjustments are needed to your long-term plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Your pain is much better, and you’re tolerating food. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m feeling more like myself. Should I watch for any warning signs at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If you develop fever, worsening pain, yellow skin, or vomiting, come back right away. Otherwise, finish all the antibiotics and keep your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my urine bacteria—should I worry about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get the full culture results. If it’s a true infection, your doctor may treat it after discharge. For now, it’s not the priority.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take the cipro twice daily for 12 days, continue all your other meds, and see your GI doctor in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), inactive IBD, celiac disease, and hypertension was admitted for acute right upper quadrant abdominal pain and fever. Initial evaluation revealed elevated liver enzymes and gallstones without cholecystitis on ultrasound. An MRCP showed progression of PSC with active bile duct inflammation but no malignancy or obstruction. She was treated with intravenous antibiotics, later transitioned to oral ciprofloxacin, and her symptoms improved significantly. She remained stable throughout the hospitalization, with no complications, and was discharged home with a 12-day course of antibiotics and instructions to follow up with her gastroenterologist in two weeks.
